To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the collective behaviour of multiple molecular motors is best understood in terms of their numbers bound to a filament.

(1) The velocity and directionality of MTs transported by multiple motors are determined by the number of motors bound to the filament, and (2) A switch-like transition from random to processive MT transport occurs when the number of motors per filament is above a critical value.
the speed, velocity and randomness of microtubule transport by yeast cytoplasm dynein are best understood in terms of the number of motors bound to the microtubule.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physical principles underlying collective transport, which may provide insight into the mechanisms underlying intracellular processes.
understanding the mechanisms of transport by multiple molecular machines.
the physical principles of collective transport and the role of stochasticity and mechanical coupling of motors in determining the directionality of transport.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the collective transport model is consistent with the data and that this model is a useful tool to understand the role of dynein in vivo.

the stochastic stepping of individual dyneins is coupled by a cooperative mechanism, that is, the number of motors attached to a microtubule is a crucial determinant for the directionality of the motion.
the stochastic stepping of individual motors can be coupled to form a collective processive motor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a stochastic stepping model with asymmetric detachment rates can explain a variety of transport phenomena in a quantitative fashion, and that this model may have relevance to a variety of other systems.
the stochastic stepping of yeast dynein motors, in combination with asymmetric detachment, can produce collective transport of microtubule filaments that are both processive and highly directional.
we show that the stochastic stepping of multiple motors is sufficient to generate a ‘switch-like’, directed transport of MTs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
collective motor transport is a complex process that depends on both the properties of the motors and their numbers.
the collective behavior of molecular motors is a key factor in determining the transport of MTs in vivo.
the stochasticity of individual motors is sufficient to explain the observed collective behaviour, without the need for additional mechanisms such as cooperative interactions or mechanical coupling.
